title: The empty throne
hookLine: early art showed the Buddha by symbols only: a footprint, a wheel, a tree, an empty seat

cards: On a carved stone panel, a crowd has gathered. People kneel with their hands together; some hold flowers. Above them spreads a great tree, every leaf cut into the stone, and beneath it is a seat, a throne with a cushion.
Everyone faces it, bowing. And the seat is empty. On panel after panel of the old railings and gateways, the scene repeats.
The Buddha's life is everywhere in the stone, and the Buddha, it seems, is nowhere.

teach.h: A TREE, A WHEEL, A FOOTPRINT.
teach.b: First, the signs. In the carvings at places like Bharhut and Sanchi, the Buddha's great moments are shown, but not him, at least not as a human figure. The awakening is a tree with an empty seat beneath it.
The first teaching is a wheel, the wheel of dhamma set turning. His presence is a pair of footprints, or a parasol held over no one. A riderless horse leaves the palace.
Every story is there, and at its center is a space.

teach.h: NO MEASURE FOR ONE GONE OUT.
teach.b: Second, the one who has gone out. The suttas don't describe these carvings, but one passage sits beside them well. In the Sutta Nipata, a seeker named Upasiva asks the Buddha what becomes of one who has reached the end.

The Buddha answers with a flame. A flame blown out by the wind comes to rest and can't be counted any more. So with the sage: there's no measure for him, nothing left by which to say he is this or that.
Some readers see the empty seat as that teaching in stone. Third, the other reading.
Some scholars suggest that some of these scenes show later pilgrims worshiping at the holy places, the tree, the seat, the footprints, rather than the Buddha's own moments with him left out.
Serious people hold both readings, and the stone itself doesn't settle it. Fourth, what the absence does. Either way, a visitor to these panels can't stare at a face.
You look at what he left: a teaching, a path, a place where someone sat down and woke up.

how: Buddhists still honor the Buddha through symbols like the wheel of dhamma, carved footprints and the bodhi tree, alongside statues, and pilgrims bow and leave offerings before them.

o: a vow of silence kept beneath the tree
a royal crown set on the Buddha's statue
a seat, here the empty one under the bodhi tree

games.q: shown by absence: tap the pairs.
p: the empty seat under a tree
asked what becomes of the one gone out

s: the old carvings at Bharhut and Sanchi leave out the Buddha's life story
his life is everywhere in the stone; it's the figure at the center that's shown by signs.
scholars all agree on why the seat is empty
some see the teaching of the one gone out; others see scenes of later pilgrims at the holy places.
the first teaching can be shown as a wheel
the wheel of dhamma, set turning.

games.q: you're a carver making a panel of the Buddha's awakening. the tree and the crowd are done. what do you put on the seat?
games.why: in the old carvings the seat is empty: the awakening is shown by the tree and the throne, and the space where he sat.

practice: With a pen on paper, or a finger on your palm, slowly draw one of the old signs: a circle with spokes for the wheel, the outline of a footprint, or a small square seat with nothing on it. Don't make it good; make it slow.
Then look at the empty part, the space inside the lines, and let that space be enough while you breathe.

wordCard.voice: Asana. The seat beneath the bodhi tree, carved empty in old reliefs, where the Buddha was shown by what he left.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Pali: asana, a seat; here, the seat beneath the bodhi tree.

carryVoice: Your line: shown by absence. A tree, a wheel, a footprint, an open seat. Until tomorrow.
